q: Walk me through the three financial statements.
a: The income statement shows revenue, costs and profit over a period, ending in net income. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, and balances. The cash flow statement starts with net income, adjusts for non-cash items and working capital to get operating cash flow, then adds investing and financing flows to explain the change in cash. Net income links to the cash flow statement and to retained earnings; ending cash links to the balance sheet.

q: Depreciation rises by Rs. 10. Walk it through the statements at a 25% tax rate.
a: Income statement: EBIT and PBT fall by 10, tax falls by 2.5, net income falls by 7.5. Cash flow: net income −7.5, add back depreciation +10, so cash rises by 2.5. Balance sheet: PP&E −10, cash +2.5, assets −7.5; retained earnings −7.5. It balances.

q: A company buys inventory of Rs. 100 on credit. What happens?
a: No income statement effect. Inventory +100 and accounts payable +100 on the balance sheet. On the cash flow statement the inventory increase (−100) and payables increase (+100) offset, so cash is unchanged.

q: What happens when the inventory is sold for Rs. 150 cash (25% tax)?
a: Revenue +150, COGS +100, PBT +50, tax +12.5, net income +37.5. Cash flow: net income +37.5 plus the inventory decrease +100, so cash +137.5. Balance sheet: cash +137.5, inventory −100, equity +37.5.

q: Why can a profitable company run out of cash?
a: Profit is recorded on accrual; cash depends on timing. Fast growth ties up cash in receivables and inventory; heavy capex, debt repayments or dividends consume cash. A company can report profits while its operating and investing cash flows are negative, and fail if it cannot fund the gap.

q: If you could use only one statement to judge a company, which would you pick?
a: The cash flow statement, because it shows whether profits turn into cash and is hardest to manipulate. I would still want the balance sheet to judge leverage and liquidity.

q: What is working capital and why does an increase use cash?
a: Operating current assets (receivables, inventory) minus operating current liabilities (payables, accruals). An increase means more cash is tied up in the operating cycle: customers owe more or stock is higher, so cash from operations falls.

q: What is deferred revenue? Give an example.
a: Cash received before the product or service is delivered, recorded as a liability. A software company billing an annual subscription upfront records deferred revenue and recognises revenue monthly as it delivers.

q: Explain the five-step model of Ind AS 115.
a: Identify the contract; identify distinct performance obligations; determine the transaction price (including variable consideration); allocate the price to each obligation using standalone selling prices; recognise revenue when or as each obligation is satisfied.

q: How did Ind AS 116 change reported numbers for a retailer or airline?
a: Operating leases came on balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and lease liability. Rent left operating expenses and was replaced by depreciation and interest, so EBITDA rose and net debt (including leases) rose; total expense is front-loaded. Operating cash flow rises because principal repayments move to financing.

q: What is goodwill and when does it change?
a: The excess of purchase price over the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired. Under Ind AS it is not amortised; it is tested for impairment at least annually and falls only when impaired, or changes with new acquisitions and disposals.

q: What are deferred tax liabilities and assets?
a: Tax effects of temporary differences between book and tax values. Faster tax depreciation than book depreciation creates a deferred tax liability; carry-forward losses and provisions not yet deductible create deferred tax assets, recognised only if future taxable profit is probable.

q: How is a 30% stake in another company accounted for? And 70%?
a: At 30% with significant influence, as an associate under the equity method: one line on the balance sheet and a share of profit in the income statement. At 70%, the company is a subsidiary: consolidate 100% of revenue, costs, assets and liabilities and show the 30% as non-controlling interest.

q: What is the difference between EBITDA and operating cash flow?
a: Operating cash flow deducts taxes paid, changes in working capital and (depending on policy) interest paid, and excludes non-cash items; EBITDA ignores all of these. EBITDA is a profitability measure; operating cash flow is a cash measure.

q: A company capitalises Rs. 50 of costs it used to expense. What happens this year and later?
a: This year EBITDA and profit rise by 50 (before tax), operating cash flow rises and investing cash flow falls by 50, so total cash is unchanged. In later years depreciation or amortisation of the capitalised amount reduces profit. Rising capitalisation with flat revenue is a quality-of-earnings red flag.

q: What would you check if receivables grew twice as fast as revenue?
a: Changes in credit terms, customer concentration and ageing, channel stuffing near period end, revenue recognition policy changes, related party sales, and provisions for doubtful debts. Then look for the effect on operating cash flow.

q: What is the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
a: Equity value is the value of shareholders' claims; enterprise value is the value of the operating business to all capital providers. EV = equity value + debt + preference capital + NCI + leases − cash and non-operating assets (such as associates).

q: Why do we subtract cash when calculating enterprise value?
a: Cash is a non-operating asset that a buyer effectively gets back; EV measures the operating business. Cash also offsets debt, so net debt is what matters.

q: Why is minority interest added to enterprise value?
a: Consolidated EBITDA includes 100% of subsidiaries even when the parent owns less. To keep EV/EBITDA consistent, EV must include the value of the minority's share.

q: A company issues Rs. 100 of new shares and holds the cash. What happens to EV and equity value?
a: Equity value rises by 100; cash rises by 100, so EV is unchanged. EV changes only when the operating business changes value or claims are mispriced.

q: Can enterprise value be negative?
a: Yes, if cash and non-operating assets exceed market value of equity plus debt, which suggests the market doubts the cash is accessible or expects losses. It is rare and usually temporary.

q: How do you calculate diluted shares?
a: Use the treasury stock method for in-the-money options and warrants: assume exercise and use the proceeds to buy back shares at the current price. Add shares from convertibles if converting is favourable (if-converted method). Use diluted shares for both market value and per-share values.

q: What multiple would you use with enterprise value, and why not P/E?
a: EV multiples pair with metrics available to all capital providers: EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, EV/revenue. P/E is an equity multiple and is affected by leverage and interest, so it can mislead when capital structures differ.

q: What are the main valuation methods, and when would you use each?
a: DCF (intrinsic value from cash flows; best for stable, forecastable businesses), trading comparables (what the market pays for peers; quick, market-based), precedent transactions (what acquirers paid, including control; for M&A). Asset-based and sum-of-the-parts for holding companies and asset-heavy firms; P/B for banks.

q: Why do precedent transactions usually give higher values than trading comps?
a: They include a control premium for the right to direct the business and capture synergies, and they reflect competitive bidding.

q: How do you choose comparable companies?
a: Same business model and end markets, similar growth and margins, similar size and geography, same accounting basis. Start from the company's stated competitors, recent IPO documents and broker coverage; prune outliers.

q: Two companies have the same P/E but different EV/EBITDA. Why?
a: Differences in leverage (net debt versus net cash), capital intensity (D&A), tax rates or non-operating income. EV/EBITDA looks through capital structure and D&A; P/E does not.

q: What drives a company's P/E multiple?
a: Growth, return on capital (which determines how much must be reinvested to grow) and risk (cost of equity). For a stable company, forward P/E = payout ratio ÷ (cost of equity − growth).

q: How do you value a bank? Why not a DCF on free cash flow to the firm?
a: Banks use debt as raw material, so FCFF and WACC are not meaningful. Use P/B against ROE (justified P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g)), residual income, dividend discount or FCFE models, with asset quality and capital adequacy as key inputs.

q: How would you value a loss-making startup?
a: Revenue multiples against comparable companies or funding rounds; a DCF built on a steady-state margin reached in future and discounted at a high rate; or venture method (exit value in 5 to 7 years discounted at a target return, adjusted for dilution).

q: What is a football field?
a: A chart that shows valuation ranges from different methods side by side against the current or offer price, used to present a range and support a recommendation.

q: Walk me through a DCF.
a: Forecast free cash flow to the firm for 5 to 10 years (EBIT after tax + D&A − capex − increase in NWC), discount at WACC, add the present value of a terminal value (perpetuity growth or exit multiple) to get EV, subtract net debt and other claims to get equity value, and divide by diluted shares.

q: How do you calculate WACC?
a: WACC = E/(D+E) × cost of equity + D/(D+E) × pre-tax cost of debt × (1 − tax), using target market-value weights. Cost of equity from CAPM: risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium.

q: What risk-free rate and equity risk premium would you use in India?
a: The 10-year government bond yield (about 7.1 to 7.2% in late September 2026). An ERP of around 6 to 8%; Damodaran's January 2026 total ERP for India is 7.08%. Be consistent to avoid double counting country risk.

q: Why do you unlever and relever beta?
a: Observed betas include the effect of each company's leverage. Unlevering removes it to get asset beta, which is comparable across peers; relevering at the target's capital structure gives the right equity beta for the company being valued.

q: Can beta be negative?
a: Yes, if an asset tends to rise when the market falls, such as some gold miners or hedging instruments. Operating companies rarely have negative betas.

q: Would you rather use perpetuity growth or an exit multiple for terminal value?
a: Use both and reconcile. Perpetuity growth ties to fundamentals but is sensitive to g and WACC; an exit multiple is market-based but imports current sentiment. Check the implied multiple from the growth method and the implied growth from the multiple.

q: What terminal growth rate would you use for an Indian company? Nominal or real?
a: Nominal, to match nominal cash flows and WACC. Typically 5 to 7%, not above long-run nominal GDP growth, and consistent with reinvestment: reinvestment rate = g ÷ return on new capital.

q: When can the cost of debt exceed the cost of equity?
a: In theory not for the same company, since equity is riskier. It can appear so in practice for distressed companies whose debt trades at high yields while stale betas understate equity risk, or when historical coupons are compared with a CAPM estimate. The correct response is to fix the cost of equity.

q: FCFF versus FCFE: when would you use each, and do they give the same value?
a: FCFF (before debt flows) discounted at WACC gives EV; FCFE (after interest and net borrowing) discounted at the cost of equity gives equity value. With consistent assumptions about leverage they should give the same equity value. FCFE is preferred for banks and when leverage is changing.

q: How do you get FCFE from the balance sheet and income statement?
a: FCFE = net income + D&A − capex − increase in NWC + net borrowing. From the balance sheet: capex = change in net PP&E + depreciation; NWC change from current assets and liabilities excluding cash and debt; net borrowing from the change in debt.

q: What happens to a DCF value if the tax rate rises?
a: Two effects: lower after-tax operating cash flow (reduces value) and a larger interest tax shield (slightly lowers WACC, increases value). The first usually dominates.

q: What is the mid-year convention?
a: Discounting each year's cash flow by half a year less, because cash arrives through the year rather than at year end. It raises value slightly.

q: NPV or IRR: which is better for choosing between mutually exclusive projects?
a: NPV, because it measures value created in rupees at the right cost of capital. IRR can mis-rank projects with different scale or timing, can have multiple solutions, and assumes reinvestment at the IRR.

q: What does the RBI's repo rate do, and where is it now?
a: It is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks overnight against government securities, and it anchors short-term rates. It was 5.25% with a neutral stance after the August 2026 policy; check the October 2026 decision.

q: How do rising interest rates affect equity valuations?
a: Higher discount rates lower the present value of future cash flows, hurting long-duration (high-growth) stocks most; borrowing costs rise; and bonds become more attractive relative to equities.

q: The rupee depreciates 5%. Who wins and who loses?
a: Exporters (IT services, pharma, textiles) gain rupee revenue; importers (oil marketers, airlines, electronics) face higher costs; companies with unhedged foreign currency debt lose; inflation pressure may rise.

q: What is the relationship between bond prices and yields? What is duration?
a: They move inversely. Modified duration is the approximate percentage change in price for a 1% change in yield; longer maturity and lower coupons mean higher duration.

q: Explain put-call parity.
a: For European options with the same strike and expiry: call − put = spot − present value of strike. A long call plus cash equal to PV(K) has the same payoff as a long put plus the stock.

q: If you expect rate cuts, would you pay or receive fixed in an overnight indexed swap?
a: Receive fixed. You lock in today's fixed rate and pay the floating rate, which falls if cuts happen.

q: What is the yen carry trade, and why does it matter for India?
a: Borrowing in low-yielding yen to invest in higher-yielding assets. When Japanese rates rise or the yen strengthens, positions unwind, causing global risk-off moves that can hit emerging market equities and currencies, including India.

q: Walk me through an IPO in India.
a: Appoint BRLMs, counsel and auditors; due diligence and DRHP; file with SEBI and exchanges; address SEBI observations; file the RHP; roadshows and price band; anchor book a day before; three-day bidding by QIBs, NIIs and retail through ASBA; pricing and prospectus; allotment T+1, credit T+2, listing T+3; lock-ins and monitoring of proceeds.

q: What is the difference between a fresh issue and an offer for sale?
a: A fresh issue creates new shares and the money goes to the company, diluting existing holders; an OFS sells existing shares and the money goes to the selling shareholders, with no change in total shares.

q: What is an anchor investor?
a: A qualified institutional buyer allotted shares at a fixed price one working day before an IPO opens, up to 60% of the QIB portion, with lock-ins (50% for 30 days, 50% for 90 days). Anchors signal quality to the rest of the book.

q: When is an acquisition accretive?
a: When the acquirer's pro forma EPS exceeds its standalone EPS. For all-stock deals, when the acquirer's P/E exceeds the P/E paid; for debt or cash deals, when the target's earnings yield exceeds the after-tax cost of debt or forgone interest.

q: A company with a P/E of 15 buys a company with a P/E of 25 in an all-stock deal. What is the combined P/E?
a: Between 15 and 25, weighted by earnings: combined market value ÷ combined earnings. The deal is EPS-dilutive for the acquirer before synergies.

q: What is in a CIM versus a teaser?
a: A teaser is a short, anonymous summary to generate interest and NDAs. A CIM is a detailed confidential document (business, market, operations, management, financials and projections) to support non-binding bids.

q: What triggers an open offer in India?
a: Acquiring 25% or more of voting rights, or control, of a listed company, or creeping acquisitions above 5% a year for holders between 25% and the maximum non-public shareholding. The open offer must be for at least 26% more of the shares, at a price no lower than regulatory benchmarks.

q: How would you advise a promoter who wants to raise Rs. 500 crore quickly for a listed company?
a: A QIP if institutional demand exists and speed matters; a rights issue if the promoter wants to maintain their stake and shareholders support it; a preferential allotment if a strategic investor is ready. Compare speed, discount, dilution, disclosure and investor quality.

q: What makes a deal fail between signing and closing?
a: Regulatory approvals (CCI, RBI, sector regulators) refused or delayed; conditions precedent not met; financing failures; a material adverse change; litigation; market moves in stock deals.

q: Why investment banking and not consulting?
a: Frame positively: you want to execute transactions with real money and measurable outcomes, go deep on valuation and capital markets, and build a sector franchise. Tie it to a concrete experience.

q: How will you handle the hours?
a: Give evidence from past high-intensity periods (audit busy season, a product launch, exams), how you managed energy and quality, and why the work motivates you. Avoid bravado.

q: Tell me about a deal our bank did recently.
a: Facts, rationale, valuation, structure, market reaction and your view, in three minutes. Mention the bank's role and what made it notable.

q: Sales grew but profit fell. How would you investigate?
a: Separate price, volume and mix; check gross margin (input costs, pricing lag, mix); check operating costs (marketing, people, freight, new capacity); check one-offs and accounting changes; quantify each driver and recommend actions.

q: What is the difference between a budget and a rolling forecast?
a: The budget (AOP) is a fixed annual plan used for targets and resource allocation; a rolling forecast is updated regularly for a fixed horizon ahead and is used for decisions on the latest information.

q: Explain price, volume and mix variances.
a: Volume variance values the change in total units at budget average price; mix variance captures the shift between products at budget prices; price variance values the change in price on actual volumes. Together they explain the revenue gap.

q: What is zero-based budgeting and when would you use it?
a: Justifying every cost from zero against its purpose, instead of adjusting last year's budget. Useful for overhead cost programmes; costly and risky if applied bluntly to capability-building spend.

q: How would you evaluate a capex proposal?
a: Strategic fit, demand and capacity assumptions, NPV and IRR against a risk-appropriate hurdle, payback, sensitivities on key drivers, funding and alternatives (lease, buy, phase), and a post-investment review plan.

q: What does a 13-week cash forecast tell you that the P&L does not?
a: The timing of cash receipts and payments week by week, including tax, capex and debt service, so that liquidity gaps can be managed before they happen.

q: How would you hedge a dollar payable due in three months?
a: Buy dollars forward to lock the rupee cost; or buy a call option on dollars to cap the cost while keeping upside; or use a natural hedge if the company has dollar receivables of similar timing.

q: A distributor asks for 60 days' credit instead of 30. How would you decide?
a: Compare the incremental contribution from any genuinely additional volume with the cost of funding the extra receivables and the added credit risk; consider precedent for other distributors; recommend a conditional agreement tied to volume and security.

q: How does Ind AS 116 affect covenants based on net debt/EBITDA?
a: Both EBITDA and debt rise; the ratio can move either way. Many loan agreements define covenants on a "frozen GAAP" or pre-Ind AS 116 basis; check the definitions.

q: Why corporate finance and not banking?
a: You want to own decisions and see their results over years, work across functions, and build towards a CFO or business leadership role. Anchor it in an experience of making or influencing a business decision.

q: Walk me through an LBO.
a: A sponsor buys a company using significant debt and some equity; the company's cash flows repay debt over the hold; the sponsor exits after 3 to 7 years. Returns come from EBITDA growth, debt paydown and any change in multiple; the key outputs are IRR and MOIC.

q: Paper LBO: EBITDA Rs. 100 crore, 10x entry, 5x debt, 10% EBITDA growth, exit at 10x in five years, about Rs. 225 crore of cumulative debt paydown. What are the returns?
a: Entry EV 1,000, debt 500, equity about 520 including fees. Exit EBITDA ≈ 161, EV ≈ 1,610, debt ≈ 275, equity ≈ 1,335. MOIC ≈ 2.6x; IRR ≈ 21%.

q: What are the main drivers of returns in an LBO?
a: Entry price, EBITDA growth (revenue and margin), debt paydown from free cash flow, leverage, exit multiple and holding period.

q: What is carried interest? What is a hurdle? What is a clawback?
a: Carry is the GP's share of profits (commonly 20%); the hurdle is the minimum return (commonly 8%) LPs receive before carry; clawback requires the GP to return carry received early if the fund's overall returns fall below the terms.

q: What is the difference between IRR and MOIC, and why track both?
a: IRR is time-weighted; MOIC is total value ÷ invested. A quick flip can show a high IRR on little money; a long hold can show a good MOIC with a mediocre IRR. LPs need both.

q: What are first close and final close?
a: First close is when a fund has enough commitments to start investing; final close is when fund-raising ends, often 12 to 18 months later, with later investors typically paying a catch-up.

q: What makes a good private equity investment?
a: A strong business (market position, recurring revenue, cash conversion), identifiable value creation levers, a management team you can back, a sensible entry price, and a clear exit path.

q: How would you do due diligence on a consumer brand?
a: Market and category growth, brand strength (share, pricing, repeat purchase), channel mix and economics, unit economics after marketing, supply chain and working capital, management, quality of earnings, and risks (competition, input costs, quick commerce disruption).

q: How is growth equity different from a buyout?
a: Growth equity takes minority stakes in growing companies, uses little or no leverage, and relies on growth and governance rights (board seats, vetoes, exit rights); buyouts take control and use leverage and operational change.

q: Why is India's PE market mostly minority growth rather than buyouts?
a: Promoter-controlled businesses reluctant to cede control, historically limited bank acquisition finance, a deep public market for exits, and fast growth that rewards growth capital. Buyouts are rising with generational change, MNC carve-outs and RBI's 2026 acquisition finance directions.

q: Why private equity and not public markets?
a: You want influence over the business (board seats, value creation), longer horizons and deep diligence, not trading on public information. Tie it to an experience of improving a business or analysing one deeply.

q: A startup raises Rs. 20 crore at an Rs. 80 crore pre-money. What does the investor own?
a: Post-money 100; investor owns 20%.

q: What is the option pool shuffle?
a: Creating or enlarging the ESOP pool in the pre-money, so existing shareholders bear its dilution and the effective pre-money is lower than the headline.

q: Explain a 1x non-participating liquidation preference.
a: On a sale, the investor receives the greater of its investment back or its pro rata share of proceeds as if converted. It protects the investor in modest exits.

q: What is the power law, and how does it change how VCs invest?
a: A few investments generate most returns. VCs therefore back companies that could become very large, seek meaningful ownership, and reserve capital to follow on in winners, accepting many failures.

q: Which metrics would you look at for a B2B SaaS startup?
a: ARR and growth, net and gross revenue retention, gross margin, CAC payback, burn multiple, logo churn, sales cycle and pipeline, and the Rule of 40 at scale.

q: What is net revenue retention, and is 105% good?
a: Revenue this year from last year's customers ÷ their revenue last year, including expansion and churn. 105% is acceptable for SME software; enterprise software leaders are well above 110 to 120%.

q: How would you size the market for a startup?
a: Bottom-up: number of target customers × realistic price per year, narrowed to those reachable today (SAM) and a plausible share (SOM); cross-check top-down.

q: What instruments do Indian startups use to raise money?
a: Equity and, mostly, compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) for investors; convertible notes for eligible startups; SAFE-like instruments structured as CCPS. US SAFEs are not directly used by Indian companies.

q: Pitch me a startup you would invest in.
a: Company, customer and problem; insight and why now; bottom-up market size and expansion; team edge; traction and retention; key risk and how you would test it; fit with the fund.

q: Why venture capital?
a: Specific evidence of spending time with founders and startups (working at one, angel investing, a market map, a newsletter), and why you prefer early-stage judgement over later-stage analysis.

q: Tell me about yourself.
a: The 90-second story: background, what pulled you towards this role, what you have done about it, why this role, why this firm. End with a hook the interviewer can follow.

q: Why this firm?
a: Something specific and true: a sector strength, a deal, a person you spoke to, a way of working. Show that you researched them and not just the industry.

q: What is your biggest weakness?
a: A real weakness relevant to the job, what it has cost you, and what you are doing about it, with evidence of improvement.

q: Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
a: A real mistake with consequences, your ownership of it, how you fixed it, and what you changed. Avoid mistakes that were someone else's fault.

q: Describe an ethical dilemma you faced.
a: A situation with genuine tension (pressure from a senior, a client request), how you reasoned, what you did, and the outcome. Interviewers in markets and funds weigh this heavily.

q: Do you invest? How do you pick stocks?
a: Be honest. Describe your process (screens, reading filings and concalls, valuation discipline), one winner and one loser, and what you learned. If you do not invest, explain how you are building the habit.

q: What other firms are you interviewing with?
a: Be truthful and consistent: name the category ("other ECM-focused banks") and explain why this firm is your preference.

q: Where do you see yourself in ten years?
a: A direction consistent with the role (senior banker, investor, CFO), with honesty about uncertainty and interest in growing within the firm.

q: Do you have any questions for us?
a: Always. Ask about the team's recent work, what distinguishes strong performers, how associates are staffed, or the interviewer's own path. Never ask about something easily found online.
